naslov: How the Knicks' season, title defense got chaotic -- fast
tekst:
THE VISUAL WAS  telling, if not stark.
The Philadelphia 76ers moved the ball all over their NBA Cup-adorned court while the New York Knicks scrambled to catch up, reminiscent of how the reigning champions ran things in the second round of last season's playoffs when they won 15 of their final 16 games, including 13 straight.
This time, the Knicks weren't taking over Xfinity Mobile Arena. They didn't get 3-pointers from Josh Hart or Miles McBride or Jalen Brunson after good ball movement. Instead, 76ers star Tyrese Maxey was driving down the lane for an easy dunk.
Sixers fans chanted "MVP" for Maxey instead of being drowned out by their rivals who made the trek down I-95. LeBron James, after a tip-in that sealed the game, basked in the love as the newest addition to this rivalry. And after Philadelphia handed New York its fourth loss of the season (98-93) on Friday night, Hart carried a bloody bruise atop his freshly braided head.
Heavy is the head that wears the crown.
If "easy" was the word used to describe the Knicks' spring, they haven't had a moment of ease since. Off the court, the team has been plagued by headlines about contract extension talks being paused for its stars until season's end and a championship ring controversy. On the court, they've posted a 3-4 record, ranked 22nd in offense and shot 35.7% from 3-point range, slightly above league average.
Early returns have the Knicks often looking like two different teams within the same night, sometimes the same quarter. Before, when the Knicks would go on one of those devastating runs of ball-popping offense and suffocating defense, teams would cower.
You could feel it. Momentum building, an almost inevitable feeling that everything would eventually go the Knicks' way -- a massive factor in their record 14.9-point differential in the playoffs.
Now, teams merely wait out the Knicks, knowing an opening is coming.
"One thing I see, when we get those runs, we start to look like the team we've been in the past. [Then] we get a little comfortable," Brunson said following the Knicks' 111-102 loss to the Orlando Magic on Oct. 25. "We've got to continue to put our foot on the gas and execute like we did last year."
Coach Mike Brown didn't deny his team has gotten off to a lethargic start. His task of getting this team to repeat as champions is tough enough: The parity era of eight champions in the past eight years is the longest such stretch in NBA history. Only last season's Thunder even made it out of the second round in pursuit of defending their title. 
It could be the competition catching up to the Knicks, or the uncertainty of player contracts having a very human effect. But to his credit, Brown is focusing on the long game and not the panic that can set in with a misfortunate start to the season.
"This is a new season. It's a new team, and we're going to have challenges in front of us," Brown said. "It's like climbing a mountain. You know, sometimes you go 100 yards, but you might get knocked back 5 yards.
"You regroup as a team, and you figure out how to keep going forward the right way by making sure we embrace the process."
IT'S NOT UNCOMMON  to see Hart stewing after a bad game or a bad stretch. More than his buddy-cop relationship with Brunson, he is the emotional center of the Knicks and has been since he arrived in 2023 at the trade deadline.
When the Knicks lost three straight games late last season, culminating in a 17-point road loss to the Rockets in Houston, Hart called it out, claiming the next night in Memphis was a must-win game.
"We're not going in the right direction," he said that evening.
The Knicks responded by winning the next five games before resting their regulars in the season finale, paving the way for their dominant playoff run.
Hart doesn't mind saying the uncomfortable thing. But with his contract status up in the air, will he hesitate should an issue arise?
"I guarantee you, I'm going to be sitting here rock bottom," Hart told ESPN. "I don't think I'm ever going to be on my high horse, either.
"We're in New York. Everything rides on the next game. We go on a 10-game winning streak and the next game we lose, they're ready to burn the place down. We know what it is. It's the tough part of being in New York."
Boston Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla, whose team handed the Knicks their second loss of this season, understands how hard it is to move past a loss.
"I don't think the psychological wars ever end after a game, I think it goes on for you as long as you're in it," Mazzulla said. "Every team brings in scars from the past."
Brown has pointed to on-ball defense, indecision on offense and his players standing around when plays break down as culprits for the slow start. According to NBA.com, the Knicks trail only the Houston Rockets and Charlotte Hornets in frequency of shots late in the shot clock (four seconds or less), and shooting 28.8% in those situations ranks them behind only the Portland Trail Blazers in efficiency -- they were best in the league last season.
Usually, that's Brunson time, as he did so often in the playoffs. But the magic hasn't been there to start the season.
The Knicks haven't come back from big deficits the way they did last season, when they rallied from double-digits in six playoff games, the largest being a 29-point comeback over the San Antonio Spurs to win Game 4 of the Finals.
Have they lulled themselves into a false sense of security with all those improbable comebacks? Will they dig themselves a hole too deep to emerge, and what's the cost of playing that way consistently?
"I've said in the past it's important to learn from wins; obviously, you learn from losses as well," Brunson said Friday in Philadelphia. "There's been plenty of times we learned from being down what we can do. And in that same game, made adjustments to where we weren't down anymore. We have to put a full 48 minutes together."
